query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short high-temperature partial solution-annealing followed by a moderate aging treatment will refine and partially homogenize the lamellar B2 phase in a eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby reducing dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, alleviating local stress concentrations, and suppressing microcrack nucleation. This modification is expected to yield an increase in both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure (fcc/B2) in which dislocation pile-ups at the coarse or strongly ordered B2 lamellae produce local stress concentrations and microcracking during room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a short high-temperature partial solution-annealing step (~1150 °C for ~30 min) followed by a moderate aging treatment (~700–800 °C for 2–4 h).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests conducted at a strain rate of approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹ under ambient conditions; the heat treatments should be performed under controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined B2 lamellae with more coherent or semi-coherent interlamellar boundaries, leading to a reduced hardness mismatch and alleviated stress concentration at phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The intervention partially homogenizes the B2 phase, reducing the disparity in mechanical properties across the lamellae and thereby enhancing dislocation transmission across the internal interfaces. This decreases dislocation pile-ups that would otherwise cause high local stresses, microcrack initiation, and catastrophic failure during straining. Subsequent aging re-establishes a fine distribution of strengthening precipitates to help maintain or enhance overall alloy strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy (~944 MPa UTS and ~25% elongation), the intervention is predicted to increase tensile strength to approximately 1000–1050 MPa and ductility to around 28–32% at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with inherent dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries leading to limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the treatment may depend on precise control of the heat-treatment durations and temperatures. If the solution-annealing step over-homogenizes the microstructure or if the aging step fails to adequately precipitate strengthening phases, the expected improvements might not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the ductility and strength enhancement is subject to variation based on minor changes in thermal processing parameters and the intrinsic stability of the dual-phase structure. Further, while the hypothesis predicts improved boundary coherence and reduced local cracking, the interplay between phase coarsening and long-term stability under cyclic loading remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same batch of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set undergoes the described two-step thermal treatment, while the second set serves as the untreated baseline. Conduct detailed microstructural analyses using TEM/EBSD to assess the coherence and spacing of B2 lamellae. Subsequently, perform room-temperature tensile tests under identical conditions (strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 25 °C).
measurements: Quantitative measurement of interfacial coherence and lamellar spacing via TEM/EBSD.
Room-temperature tensile properties: ultimate tensile strength and tensile elongation.
Assessment of crack initiation sites and microcracking via fractography after tensile testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in tensile strength (target ≥1000 MPa) and ductility (target ≥28% elongation), or if microstructural characterization reveals no enhancement in interface coherence (i.e., if dislocation pile-ups and microcrack nucleation remain unchanged compared to the untreated baseline), then the hypothesis that the specific thermal treatment mitigates brittle failure by refining the lamellar boundaries must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: Among the surveyed works, only PMC4145285 explicitly investigated a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with dual-phase lamellar colonies and addressed simultaneously achieving strength and ductility in a cast microstructure. That paper showed that as-cast lamellar EHEAs can sustain moderate-to-high ultimate strengths (≈944 MPa) with good tensile elongation (≈25.6%). Limited cold rolling raised strength but significantly sacrificed ductility, caused by strain localization and boundary-related microcrack initiation. While ductility remains acceptable for some conditions in that system, mitigating brittle fracture associated with lamellar boundaries and local stress concentrations remains an open challenge in many EHEAs.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in balancing strength and ductility through minor cold working or conventional heat treatments, it remains difficult to suppress dislocation pile-ups and microcracking at the fine B2/fcc interfaces under room-temperature tensile loading without decreasing overall strength. Ensuring that boundary modifications (e.g., refining lamellae or tuning interface chemistry) can mitigate these local failure mechanisms while preserving the alloy’s hierarchical architecture remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Apply a short high-temperature partial solution-annealing step (e.g., ~1150 °C for ~30 min) followed by a moderate aging treatment (e.g., ~700–800 °C for 2–4 h) to partially homogenize and refine the B2 lamellae, stabilizing a more ductile, coherent or semi-coherent interface structure.
decision.why: Prior evidence (PMC4145285) indicates that lamellar EHEAs can achieve excellent mechanical properties but remain susceptible to boundary-induced crack initiation under tension. A brief solution anneal near 1150 °C can disrupt coarse or strongly ordered B2 lamellae, reducing their hardness mismatch with adjacent fcc (or disordered) domains and alleviating local stress concentrations. A subsequent moderate-temperature aging step can re-form finer, more uniformly distributed B2 precipitates to maintain or slightly enhance strength. Relative to the starting EHEA (UTS ~944 MPa, ductility ~25%), this approach is predicted to increase both tensile strength (to ~1000–1050 MPa) and ductility (to ~28–32%) at room temperature. These gains should be validated using standard tensile tests (e.g., strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 25 °C). A falsification experiment would be to measure the resulting lamellar boundary character (via TEM or EBSD) and confirm whether post-anneal microcrack nucleation sites decrease. If boundary-mitigated cracking still dominates or ductility does not improve in mechanical tests, the hypothesis that refining or partially homogenizing B2 lamellae enhances ductility while retaining strength would be disproven.
